title: Clarity & Concision

learn.summary: Strunk & White's most famous command — 'Omit needless words' — and Zinsser's diagnosis that 'clutter is the disease of American writing' point at the same discipline: every word must do work. Clarity is not dumbing down; it is respect for the reader's time and proof that you know what you mean. Simplify first; style comes later and only survives on a clear base.

do: Take any 300-word passage you wrote and cut it to 200 words without losing a single idea.

children.title: Cutting Clutter

learn.summary: Zinsser's clutter list is a field guide: qualifiers ('a bit', 'sort of'), throat-clearing ('it should be noted that'), redundant pairs ('each and every'), and prepositional fat ('at this point in time' for 'now'). His classroom method was brutal and effective — bracket every word that does no work, then read the sentence without the brackets. Most professional prose survives a 30% cut and improves.

do: Bracket every removable word in one page of your writing, then delete the brackets' contents and compare versions aloud.

children.title: Active Voice

learn.summary: 'The committee approved the budget' beats 'the budget was approved by the committee': shorter, clearer about who acted, and more energetic. Strunk & White's 'use the active voice' is the right default, but not a ban — passive earns its place when the actor is unknown or irrelevant ('the samples were heated to 90°C'). The real sin is passive-as-evasion: 'mistakes were made'.

do: Search one document for 'was', 'were', and 'been'; convert every evasive or flabby passive to active, keeping only justified ones.

children.title: Concrete Nouns, Strong Verbs

learn.summary: Abstractions ('utilization', 'implementation') hide meaning; concrete nouns and vivid verbs carry it. The worst offender is nominalization — burying the verb inside a noun: 'make a decision' for 'decide', 'conduct an investigation' for 'investigate'. Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language' shows where this leads: prose built from prefabricated abstract phrases that thinks for you, badly.

do: Hunt one page for buried verbs ('-tion', '-ment', '-ance' nouns) and un-bury five of them into direct verbs.

children.title: Jargon & Cliché

learn.summary: Jargon is fine between specialists and fatal everywhere else; the test is whether your named reader uses the term unprompted. Clichés ('low-hanging fruit', 'at the end of the day') are worse than plain words because they signal the writer stopped thinking mid-sentence — Orwell's rule: never use a figure of speech you are used to seeing in print. Plain-language research by governments shows plain rewrites measurably improve comprehension and compliance.

do: Collect the 10 jargon terms and clichés you use most (search old emails), and write a plain replacement for each.
